title: Jude

stories.title: 📜 Jude
summaryBullets: Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James, To those who are called, loved by God the Father, and kept in Jesus Christ: (1:1).
Mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you. (1:2).

Beloved, although I made every effort to write to you about the salvation we share, I felt it necessary to write and urge you to contend earnestly for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints. (1:3).

For certain men have crept in among you unnoticed — ungodly ones who were designated long ago for condemnation. They turn the grace of our God into a license for immorality, and they deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ. (1:4).
Although you are fully aware of this, I want to remind you that after Jesus had delivered His people out of the land of Egypt, He destroyed those who did not believe. (1:5).
And the angels who did not stay within their own domain but abandoned their proper dwelling— these He has kept in eternal chains under darkness, bound for judgment on that great day. (1:6).

In like manner, Sodom and Gomorrah and the cities around them, who indulged in sexual immorality and pursued strange flesh, are on display as an example of those who sustain the punishment of eternal fire. (1:7).
Yet in the same way these dreamers defile their bodies, reject authority, and slander glorious beings. (1:8).
But even the archangel Michael, when he disputed with the devil over the body of Moses, did not presume to bring a slanderous charge against him, but said, “The Lord rebuke you!” (1:9).
These men, however, slander what they do not understand, and like irrational animals, they will be destroyed by the things they do instinctively. (1:10).
Woe to them! They have traveled the path of Cain; they have rushed for profit into the error of Balaam; they have perished in Korah’s rebellion. (1:11).

These men are hidden reefs in your love feasts, shamelessly feasting with you but shepherding only themselves. They are clouds without water, carried along by the wind; fruitless trees in autumn, twice dead after being uprooted. (1:12).
They are wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shame; wandering stars, for whom blackest darkness has been reserved forever. (1:13).
Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied about them: “Behold, the Lord is coming with myriads of His holy ones (1:14).
to execute judgment on everyone, and to convict all the ungodly of every ungodly act of wickedness and every harsh word spoken against Him by ungodly sinners.” (1:15).
These men are discontented grumblers, following after their own lusts; their mouths spew arrogance; they flatter others for their own advantage. (1:16).
But you, beloved, remember what was foretold by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ (1:17).
when they said to you, “In the last times there will be scoffers who will follow after their own ungodly desires.” (1:18).
These are the ones who cause divisions, who are worldly and devoid of the Spirit. (1:19).
But you, beloved, by building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, (1:20).
keep yourselves in the love of God as you await the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ to bring you eternal life. (1:21).
And indeed, have mercy on those who doubt; (1:22).
save others by snatching them from the fire; and to still others show mercy tempered with fear, hating even the clothing stained by the flesh. (1:23).
Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you unblemished in His glorious presence, with great joy — (1:24).
to the only God our Savior be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority through Jesus Christ our Lord before all time, and now, and for all eternity. Amen. (1:25).

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: לְהִלָּחֵם עַל־הָאֱמוּנָה (lehillāḥēm ʿal-hāʾĕmûnāh, sense), Greek: ἐπαγωνίζεσθαι τῇ πίστει (epagōnízesthai tē pístei, NT), Aramaic: לאתגוש על הימנותא (leʾitgōš ʿal heymanūṯā)
translationNotes.note: Military-style verb meaning to struggle or fight earnestly for the faith entrusted to God’s people.

translationNotes.original: Hebrew: רָשָׁע (rāšāʿ), Greek: ἀσεβεῖς (asebeîs, NT), Aramaic: רשיעיא (rešīʿayyā)
translationNotes.note: Describes those who live without reverence for God, violating his covenant and moral order.

The Old Testament does not record this dispute. Deuteronomy 34:5-6 says Moses died in Moab, that He buried him in the valley opposite Beth-peor, and that no one knows his burial place to this day. Michael is named in Daniel 10:13, 10:21, and 12:1 as the prince who stands over Israel, and again in Revelation 12:7. The words Jude gives him, 'The Lord rebuke you', are word for word what the angel of the LORD says to Satan in Zechariah 3:2. Origen, writing in the early third century, says Jude took the episode from a book called the Ascension of Moses; the surviving text of that work breaks off before any such scene, so it cannot now be read there.

Count the line in Genesis 5 and Enoch is seventh: Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch. Genesis 5:24 says he walked with God and was not, for God took him, and Hebrews 11:5 repeats it. The lines Jude quotes in verses 14 and 15 are the words of 1 Enoch 1:9, and Jude introduces them by saying Enoch prophesied them. That book was in circulation well before Jude wrote: Aramaic fragments of it were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran, Greek portions survive on papyrus, and the whole work is preserved in Ge'ez, the old language of Ethiopia. Jude says what he says about Enoch and no more.

Three men, three separate ruins, and Jude puts them in order. Cain killed his brother over an offering God had accepted and his own God had not (Genesis 4:3-8). Balaam took a fee from Balak of Moab to curse Israel, and when he could not, his counsel pulled Israel into sin at Peor instead (Numbers 22-24; 31:16). Korah, a Levite, with Dathan, Abiram, and 250 leading men, challenged the authority God had given Moses and Aaron; the ground opened and swallowed the households, and fire took the 250 men holding censers (Numbers 16:31-35).

translationNotes.term: Hidden reefs in your love feasts
translationNotes.note: The agape was the shared meal the assemblies ate together, at which the Lord's Supper was taken. It could be abused, and 1 Corinthians 11:20-22 describes exactly how: some eating ahead of the rest, some going hungry, at a table meant to be common. Roman hosts normally graded a dinner by rank, serving better food and better wine to better-placed guests, a practice Pliny the Younger describes with contempt in his letters. A spilas is a rock lying just under the surface of the water, the kind that opens a hull before the crew sees anything at all.

Planetes means wanderer, and it is the word English turned into 'planet'. Sailors and caravans held a course by the fixed stars, which keep the same positions relative to one another night after night and season after season. The wanderers drift against that pattern, so you cannot steer by one. The book Jude quotes three verses later describes stars bound in a prison for having transgressed the command of the Lord by not rising at their appointed times (1 Enoch 18:13-16).

translationNotes.term: Sodom and the cities around them
translationNotes.original: Greek: ἐκπορνεύσασαι (ekporneusasai), from ἐκπορνεύω (ekporneuo) - σαρκὸς ἑτέρας (sarkos heteras), 'other flesh'
translationNotes.note: Jude 1:7 names Sodom and Gomorrah 'and the cities around them,' which Deuteronomy 29:23 lists as Admah and Zeboiim, destroyed alongside the other two. The participle ekporneusasai is a strengthened form of the verb for sexual immorality, and the second phrase, going after sarkos heteras, is literally other or different flesh. Genesis 19:4-11 is the scene Jude is pointing at, where the men of the city surround Lot's house and demand the two visitors. Jude says the cities are set out as an example, undergoing the punishment of eternal fire.

stories.keyTakeaway: Jude exhorts believers to contend for the faith against ungodly intruders who pervert grace and deny Christ.

intro:
Jude was written by Jude, the half-brother of Jesus and brother of James (Jude 1:1: "Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James"). Jude was a son of Mary and Joseph and one of Jesus' four named brothers (James, Joseph or Joses, Simon, and Judas/Jude per Matthew 13:55 and Mark 6:3), plus unnamed sisters. Like his brother James, Jude did not believe in Jesus during Jesus' earthly ministry (John 7:5: "Even his brothers did not believe in him") but became a follower after the resurrection appearances. 1 Corinthians 9:5 mentions that "the brothers of the Lord" were married and traveled with their wives in Christian missionary work. Jude self-identifies in this letter as "brother of James" rather than as "brother of Jesus" out of humility (calling himself "a servant of Jesus Christ" instead), and by referencing his more famous brother James (the leader of the Jerusalem church and author of the Letter of James) he distinguishes himself from the other men named Jude/Judas in the early Christian community. The author of this letter must be carefully distinguished from the other men named Judas in the New Testament: he is NOT Judas Iscariot the betrayer of Jesus; he is NOT Judas son of James, the apostle (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13; John 14:22), who was also called Thaddaeus (Matthew 10:3); he is NOT Judas Barsabbas, the Jerusalem prophet sent to Antioch with Silas (Acts 15:22, 27, 32); he is NOT Judas of Galilee, the failed messianic claimant mentioned by Gamaliel (Acts 5:37). Jude is specifically the half-brother of Jesus and the full brother of James the half-brother of Jesus. The English form "Jude" (rather than "Judas") is used in most modern translations specifically to distinguish him from Judas Iscariot; both names translate the same Greek Ioudas, which is itself the Greek form of the Hebrew Yehudah ("Judah," "praise"), the name of one of the twelve patriarchs (Genesis 29:35).

The letter was composed sometime between AD 65 and AD 80, with the lower end of that range being most likely if Jude wrote before 2 Peter (or alternatively if Jude wrote first and 2 Peter drew on him); the two letters share substantial content in their denunciation of false teachers (compare 2 Peter 2 with Jude 1:4-19). The place of composition is unknown but probably somewhere in Palestine or the broader eastern Mediterranean where Jesus' family had settled. The Roman emperor was Nero (AD 54-68), Galba (AD 68-69), Otho (AD 69), Vitellius (AD 69), Vespasian (AD 69-79), or Titus (AD 79-81), depending on the precise date. According to early Christian tradition preserved by Hegesippus (recorded by Eusebius in Ecclesiastical History 3.20), two of Jude's grandsons were brought before the emperor Domitian (AD 81-96), who was investigating surviving descendants of King David as potential messianic threats to his rule; the grandsons were peasant farmers who showed their work-hardened hands and explained that the kingdom they awaited was heavenly rather than earthly, and Domitian released them as harmless. Tradition variously holds that Jude himself ministered in Mesopotamia, Persia, Armenia, and Edessa, and that he was martyred (some accounts by axe or club, in Beirut or Persia or Mesopotamia), though no consistent early account survives. The audience of the letter is general ("to those who are called, beloved in God the Father and kept for Jesus Christ," Jude 1:1) rather than a single congregation or individual; Jude wrote to address an urgent crisis affecting churches generally.

Jude is the sixty-fifth book of the Christian Bible, the twenty-sixth book of the New Testament, and the seventh and last of the General Epistles (immediately before Revelation). At twenty-five verses (one chapter), Jude is one of the shorter books of the New Testament. The earliest surviving manuscript is Papyrus 72 (P72, the Bodmer Papyrus, c. AD 250-300), the same codex that preserves 1 Peter and 2 Peter; other early witnesses include Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (both 4th century AD). Jude is notable in the New Testament for being the only book that directly quotes the apocryphal book of 1 Enoch as prophecy: Jude 1:14-15 ("It was also about these that Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying, 'Behold, the Lord comes with ten thousands of his holy ones, to execute judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly of all their deeds of ungodliness that they have committed in such an ungodly way, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him'") is a direct quotation of 1 Enoch 1:9 (the apocalyptic Jewish text traditionally attributed to Enoch the seventh from Adam, present in the Ethiopian Orthodox canon and quoted as authoritative by Jude). Jude also references the dispute between the archangel Michael and the devil over the body of Moses (Jude 1:9), which derives from the Jewish work the Assumption of Moses (or possibly the Testament of Moses), an account not preserved in the canonical Old Testament. Jude originally intended to write a general letter "about our common salvation" (Jude 1:3) but felt compelled to redirect to "contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints" because of false teachers who had "crept in unnoticed... ungodly people, who pervert the grace of our God into sensuality and deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ" (Jude 1:4). The letter closes with one of the most stirring benedictions in the New Testament (Jude 1:24-25): "Now to him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before the presence of his glory with great joy, to the only God, our Savior, through Jesus Christ our Lord, be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority, before all time and now and forever. Amen."
